title: Arrow functions versus function declarations in types
hook: Arrow functions and function declarations compile to similar JavaScript, but they differ in this binding, hoisting, and what TypeScript allows in type positions — a common source of callback bugs and interview questions.

blocks.text: **Function declarations** are hoisted and have their own **dynamic this**. **Arrow functions** (`=>`) capture **lexical this** from the enclosing scope and cannot be used as constructors. In **type positions**, both write as `(x: T) => R` — arrow syntax is required in types (no `function` keyword in type aliases). **Generator** and **async** variants follow the same runtime rules as JavaScript.

entries.plainDefinition: Concise syntax with lexical this — no own this binding.
entries.example: const add = (a: number, b: number) => a + b

entries.plainDefinition: Hoisted function with dynamic this and own arguments object in non-strict legacy.
entries.example: function add(a: number, b: number) { return a + b; }

entries.plainDefinition: this from surrounding scope — arrow functions use this.

blocks.text: React class components needed arrow handlers to preserve this; hooks eliminated many cases. `Array.prototype.map` callbacks rarely need this — arrows are fine. Object methods should use method shorthand for correct this prototype sharing. C# lambdas capture variables like JS arrows but have no this keyword.

blocks.title: Type aliases always use arrow syntax
blocks.body: type Fn = (x: number) => string — never type Fn = function(x: number): string

items.title: Class field handlers
items.body: Arrow field — lexical this for event handlers.

items.title: Generators / constructors
items.body: function* or function — arrows cannot be constructors.

diagram.title: this binding comparison
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  ARROW[arrow function] --> LEX[lexical this]
  DECL[function declaration] --> DYN[dynamic this at call site]
  METHOD[method shorthand] --> DYN

snippet.label: Type position — arrow only
snippet.explanation: Line 1: type alias requires => syntax. Line 4: implementation can be function declaration — assignable if shape matches.

snippet.label: Class — method vs arrow field
snippet.explanation: Line 5: function callback loses Timer this. Line 11: arrow captures Timer instance.

snippet.label: Concise returns and blocks
snippet.explanation: Line 1: expression body — implicit return. Line 3: block body needs explicit return and optional return type annotation.

snippet.label: Failure mode — arrow as constructor
snippet.explanation: Arrows cannot be called with new — use class or function declaration for constructors.

blocks.title: Arrow methods on prototype
blocks.body: class { m = () => {} } creates per-instance function — memory cost vs shared method.

blocks.text: Arrow functions lack arguments object (use rest). Cannot declare this parameter on arrows. Async arrows inherit async function semantics. In strict mode, nested function declarations are block-scoped (ES2015). Performance: arrow vs function negligible — choose for semantics. React useCallback returns memoized function — still mind deps array.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Using function keyword in type alias. Not knowing arrow lexical this. Creating arrow per instance without acknowledging memory tradeoff.

interviewTakeaways: Type aliases use => syntax; implementations can be arrow or function.
Arrows: lexical this. function: dynamic this.
Arrows cannot be constructors or have this parameter.
60s: Arrows for callbacks preserving this. Methods on prototype for shared behavior. Types always arrow syntax. C# lambdas capture locals not this.
commonPitfalls: Weak: function keyword in type position — use =>.
Weak: setTimeout with function callback in class — loses this.
Strong: Arrow for HOF callbacks. Method shorthand on prototype. Arrow class fields when this needed.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Arrows are runtime syntax — TS adds this-safety checks in class callbacks.
Only non-arrow functions can declare this parameter for dynamic this typing.
